content: Access to oral healthcare is often reported as poor or inequitable across countries with varying income levels. This issue is influenced by the insufficient number of dentists and their uneven distribution. Delegating certain dental tasks to dental auxiliaries has been proposed as a potential solution to improve access to care, extend services to underserved areas, and allow dentists to focus on more complex procedures. However, before endorsing this approach, it is essential to evaluate the effectiveness, costs, and cost-effectiveness of dental auxiliaries compared to dentists. To address this, a systematic review was conducted to assess the effectiveness of dental auxiliaries in performing tasks traditionally carried out by dentists. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled clinical trials (NRCTs), interrupted time series (ITSs), and controlled before-and-after studies (CBAs). The search spanned multiple electronic databases up to November 2013, including Cochrane databases, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others. Grey literature was also reviewed, and authors of relevant studies were contacted. Five studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. These studies involved 13 dental auxiliaries, six dentists, and over 1,156 participants. The clinical tasks evaluated included the placement of preventive resin fissure sealants and the atraumatic restorative technique (ART). The studies were conducted in the United States, Canada, Gambia, and Singapore. Four studies assessed the effectiveness of dental auxiliaries in placing preventive resin fissure sealants. Three of these studies found no significant difference in the retention rates of sealants placed by dental auxiliaries compared to those placed by dentists over follow-up periods ranging from six to 24 months. However, one study reported that sealants placed by dental auxiliaries had lower retention rates after 48 months (9.0% for auxiliaries versus 29.1% for dentists). This same study also found that the reduction in the number of teeth with caries after 48 months was lower for teeth treated by dental auxiliaries compared to dentists (3 teeth with auxiliaries versus 60 teeth with dentists, P < 0.001). Another study found no difference in dental decay outcomes between the two groups after treatment with fissure sealants. One study compared the effectiveness of dental auxiliaries and dentists in performing ART and found no difference in the survival rates of restorations (fillings) after 12 months. However, no studies were identified that evaluated the effectiveness of dental auxiliaries in diagnosing oral diseases, delivering oral health education, or other health promotion activities. Additionally, no studies assessed participants' perspectives, including the acceptability of care provided by dental auxiliaries, nor were there any reports of adverse effects. The overall quality of the evidence was very low, as assessed using the GRADE approach. All included studies were at high risk of bias, and four of the five studies were over 20 years old, making the materials and techniques evaluated outdated. Furthermore, no studies met the inclusion criteria for comparing the costs, cost-effectiveness, or impact on access and equity of care between dental auxiliaries and dentists. In conclusion, the review identified only five studies, all of which were of low quality and high risk of bias. The limited and outdated evidence prevents any definitive conclusions about the relative effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, or safety of dental auxiliaries compared to dentists in performing clinical tasks. High-quality research is needed to better understand the role of dental auxiliaries in oral healthcare delivery.
